opus-5.5.text:
I think domestic demand is actually the underrated piece of this. When people talk about the data industry for agents, they often frame it as a supply problem: who has the annotators, who has the RL environments, who can build the verifiers. But the reason companies like Scale AI or Surge or Mercor became so big in the US is that there was a handful of frontier labs with enormous budgets that would pay almost anything for high-quality data. That concentrated demand is what pulled the whole industry into existence.

In China the picture is a bit different. You have a lot of strong model builders: DeepSeek, Qwen at Alibaba, Moonshot, Zhipu, MiniMax, and others. But historically many of them have been more cost-conscious, and there's been a strong culture of doing things in-house, leaning on clever synthetic data and distillation rather than buying huge volumes of expert human data. That works really well for getting to a strong base model and for things like math and code where you can verify answers. It's harder for agents, where you need realistic environments, long-horizon tasks, tool-use traces, and domain-specific workflows that look like actual work people do.

So the question becomes: is there enough domestic demand to justify building that specialized layer? I think the answer is increasingly yes, and it comes from a few places. One is the consumer and enterprise app ecosystem in China, which is huge and very fast at deploying things. If companies are actually putting agents into products, into e-commerce, customer service, coding tools, office software, they generate the demand for environments and evaluation data that mirror Chinese software, Chinese websites, Chinese business processes. You can't just import that from American vendors, both for practical reasons and for regulatory and political ones.

The second is that the open-weight strategy creates its own demand. If Chinese labs keep releasing strong open models, a lot of downstream companies will fine-tune and post-train them for specific use cases, and those companies need data and environments too. That's a broader, more distributed customer base than just a few frontier labs.

The caveat is that the very best agentic data tends to require expensive experts, and the willingness to pay for that is what really separates the tiers. If Chinese demand stays focused on cost efficiency, you might get a big, scrappy data industry that's great at volume and synthetic pipelines, but the top end of expert-crafted environments could lag. On the other hand, the Chinese labs have repeatedly shown they can get surprisingly far with less, so I wouldn't bet against them finding a different path. Domestic demand is what decides whether this becomes a real industry or stays a set of internal tools inside each lab.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that the data story in China is less about the government and more about what the market actually asks for. When you look at where the specialized data for agents comes from, it's not really the pretraining corpus, which is mostly web-scale and somewhat commoditized at this point. It's the post-training data: trajectories of a model actually doing a task, the environments it runs in, the verifiers that say whether it succeeded, and the human labels on where it went wrong. That stuff is expensive, it's narrow, and nobody builds it speculatively. You build it because there's a customer with a workflow they want automated.

So domestic demand matters in a pretty direct way. If you have a lot of companies in e-commerce, logistics, finance, customer service, manufacturing, all of them wanting agents that work inside their specific software and their specific regulatory setup, that creates a pull for data vendors and for labs to go build the environments and the evaluation harnesses for those tasks. The data industry follows the deployment surface. In the US a lot of that early pull came from coding, because developers were the first group willing to pay, and you can see how much that shaped what the models are good at. In China the surface is different, and I'd expect the data ecosystem to be shaped by that, with more weight on consumer apps and enterprise workflows that look nothing like a GitHub repo.

The other piece is that this is where the open-weight strategy and the data strategy interact. Chinese labs have been very aggressive about releasing open models, and that drives adoption, but it also means the moat shifts to the stuff you can't download: the proprietary environments, the usage data coming back from real deployments, the labeling operations you've built around your own customers. A big domestic market gives you more of that feedback loop. Whether it's enough to close the gap on the hardest frontier capabilities is a different question, because those still seem to depend on compute and on a fairly small set of research decisions. But for the long tail of "make an agent that actually works for this business," domestic demand is probably the single biggest input into what data gets built, and I think people underrate how much of agent capability is just that long tail done well.

astra-6.text:
I think domestic demand is what makes that industry viable. You need companies deploying agents on real tasks, discovering where they fail, and then paying for data that addresses those failures. That creates a feedback loop between the people using the systems and the people producing the training data.

For agents, that data goes beyond labeling an answer as good or bad. You need examples of how to complete a workflow, how to use the relevant tools, and how to recover when something goes wrong. A lot of that knowledge is specific to an industry, or even to one company’s internal processes.

So for China, the question is how much domestic adoption turns into sustained spending on those capabilities. Chinese-language workflows and local software create reasons to build specialized data locally. But a large potential market doesn’t automatically produce a strong data industry. Customers have to see enough value in the agents to pay for better performance, and suppliers need a way to demonstrate that their data actually delivers it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think domestic demand is what makes that industry viable. If Chinese companies are deploying agents in real workflows—customer support, software development, manufacturing—they create demand for data that reflects those workflows. That’s much more specific than collecting a large amount of text from the internet. You need examples of how to use tools, how to handle exceptions, and how to tell whether a task was actually completed successfully.

The important thing is the feedback loop. A customer pays for an agent, the deployment exposes where it fails, and those failures tell you what additional training data and evaluations you need. Specialized data providers can then build expertise around particular industries.

But I’d distinguish demand for impressive demos from demand for reliable products. If customers are willing to pay for measurable improvements, that can sustain a specialized data industry. A large domestic market creates the opportunity; actual adoption and willingness to pay are what turn it into a business.
